Write one deterministic regression test for Go native usage-graph cancellation (issue #5672), in the worktree you start in (branch 5672-go-graph-cancellation-test, at origin/master 20cb2116b0). Do not commit; the parent commits. Do not touch other worktrees.

Why: Go's usage graph is about to switch to the native engine by default. The owner's rule is that a cancelled request must stop. A field report (#5672) said a cancelled native Go whole-graph request kept running. On current master it does not reproduce: evaluation stops within 80-150 ms of CPU after the cancel. We need a regression test that pins the behavior before the switch.

What the test asserts (graph-level, through the native Go graph builder, not through an environment variable):
- Use a small multi-file, multi-package Go fixture project whose whole graph needs several staged batches/files and has at least a few edges. Reuse an existing Go graph test fixture if one fits; otherwise add a small one under the owning crate's test tree.
- First compute the uncancelled whole graph and keep it as the reference answer. Also assert that it is complete and non-empty.
- Then sweep `CancellationToken::cancel_after_checks_for_test(n)` (crates/bifrost-core/src/cancellation.rs:288) over a range of check counts. Use the Rust test `native_import_alternatives_share_one_terminal_budget_and_cancellation` (crates/bifrost-rust-analysis/src/analyzer/rust/native_points/tests.rs around 666-746) as the model. Use counts from 1 up past the number of checks the full run makes. Measure the full run's check count if the token exposes it; otherwise pick a geometric sweep that reaches it, and prove in the test that the largest count completes.
- For every n, the result is exactly one of: (a) a cancelled outcome, which says it was cancelled and does not claim to be a complete graph; or (b) the complete reference answer, identical to the uncancelled run. Never a partial graph that reports itself complete, never an empty complete product, and never a budget-exceeded result. Assert that at least one n gives (a) aft
